Question three. What is the difference between a transformation and an action in Spark? Transformations, like filter, group by and join, are lazy: each adds a step to a plan, and nothing runs. Here only show is an action: it makes Spark compile the plan, schedule it and run it. Count, collect and write are actions too. Question four. Why does Spark use lazy evaluation? So the optimizer sees the whole plan before anything runs, and can rewrite it. It pushes the filter into the scan, so less is read, prunes unused columns, fuses chained steps, and picks the join strategy. Run step by step, and none of that is possible.

Question five. What is a partition in Spark, and why does partition count matter? A partition is the unit of parallelism: one task works on one partition, on one core. Model it with sixteen gigabytes on sixteen cores. In four partitions of four gigabytes, twelve cores sit idle, and a partition that big can run out of memory. In a hundred thousand of a hundred sixty kilobytes, scheduling the tiny tasks costs more than their work. The rough target: a few hundred megabytes a partition, and two to four times as many partitions as cores. Sixty-four of two hundred fifty megabytes meets both. Repartition shuffles to any count. Coalesce only merges partitions, with no full shuffle: the cheap way to cut the count before writing.

Question six. What is the difference between narrow and wide dependencies? In a narrow one, like map, filter or union, each parent partition feeds at most one child: rows stay put, and steps run back to back. In a wide one, a child needs rows from many parents, as in group by key, join and distinct. That forces a shuffle.
